query: Starting from a multi-element automotive alloy catalyst containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios, what single intervention could overcome activity loss and durability limitations while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption during transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation, including exposure to H2O and NO and degradation associated with thermal aging or increasing mileage? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the untreated starting catalyst, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: The incorporation of a high-entropy alloy (HEA) as a catalyst component can overcome activity loss and durability limitations in automotive alloy catalysts while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of a high-entropy alloy (HEA) as a catalyst component
generation.conditions: Transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation, including exposure to H2O and NO
generation.mechanism: Synergistic interactions among multiple elements in the HEA, leading to enhanced catalytic activity and stability
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved catalytic activity and durability, with reduced platinum-group-metal consumption
generation.boundary: Operation under transient and low-temperature conditions, with exposure to H2O and NO
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and structure of the HEA catalyst component may affect its performance and stability

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the catalytic activity and durability of the untreated multi-element automotive alloy catalyst with that of the HEA-modified catalyst under transient and low-temperature conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA-modified catalyst does not exhibit improved catalytic activity and durability, with reduced platinum-group-metal consumption, compared to the untreated catalyst, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have emerged as an interesting class of materials with promising applications in the field of energy storage and electrocatalysis., HEAs are single-phase crystals composed of five or more principal elements in nearly equal atomic ratios, resulting in a high configurational entropy that stabilizes the structure., The possibility to tune composition and concentrations allows for detailed control of physical and chemical properties, including optimization of reaction kinetics and catalytic performance.− Many HEAs have good mechanical properties, such as enhanced hardness, superior elongation capacity, and high thermal stability, which is important to ensure long-term performance of the catalyst under harsh electrochemical conditions. Finally, the so-called cocktail effect, referring to synergistic interactions among multiple elements, can lead to emergent properties that surpass those of the individual elements, leading to superior performance, e.g., for catalyzing complex chemical reactions.

In addition to the enhanced catalytic activities, the HEA-CoxMoy catalysts were further demonstrated to be highly stable under the reaction conditions for NH3 decomposition. Figure 4f presents the NH3 conversion recorded on Co25Mo45Fe10Ni10Cu10 over the course of continuous operation at 500 oC. The degradation in catalytic activity was negligible after ~50 h. The catalyst collected after this prolonged durability test was characterized by element mapping (see the insert in Fig. 4f) and XPS (Supplementary Fig. 18), with nearly no change found in alloy homogeneity or surface composition. A small amount (~1.4 at.%) of N was detected on the used catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 19), but much less than what (e.g., >10% for Mo3Co3N) one would expect for the formation of nitrides throughout the nanoparticles. It is likely that the bulk of the HEA nanoparticles were not subjected to nitridation during the NH3 decomposition reaction. The durable performance of the HEA catalysts is in line with the reported high thermal and chemical, stabilities of HEAs.

In this paper, small PtPdCoCuNi HEA nanoparticles were successfully prepared by a one-pot solvothermal synthesis method and deposited on SiO2 to prepare a PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 catalyst with uniform dispersion of HEA nanoparticles. The catalytic performance of the PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 catalyst for nitrobenzene hydrogenation was tested and compared to counterparts with fewer metal components. The PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 catalyst exhibits high activity even at room temperature. The catalyst was characterized by a series of techniques, including HRSTEM, XRD, XPS, and DRIFTS, to obtain mechanistic understanding of the structure–activity relationship of the HEA catalyst. Both experimental and theoretical results evidence the formation of isolated Pt and Pd active sites in HEA and the resulting charge-transfer from the cheap transition metals to the noble metals, which suggests that the modulated electronic structure could promote adsorption of nitrobenzene on Pt/Pd active sites and eventually enhance nitrobenzene hydrogenation activity.
